title: How do you talk about risks in a case without sounding vague?
description: When you are asked "What are the risks?" or need to close a recommendation.
hook: Every recommendation should mention risks, but "there are some risks" does not earn any marks. Here is a quick way to list them in groups so you sound thoughtful rather than vague.
body:
When it helps

When you are asked "What are the risks?" or need to close a recommendation.

The checklist

Business

  • Demand lower than planned
  • Competitors react
  • Prices fall

Operations

  • Delays and cost overruns
  • Quality or supply problems
  • Skills we lack

Strategy

  • Distracts from the core business
  • Hurts the brand
  • Locks us in

Regulation and macro

  • Laws and approvals
  • Politics
  • Exchange rates and the economy

An example

You recommend that a coffee chain opens in Germany. Business risks: Germans may not take to the brand, local chains may cut prices. Operations: finding sites and staff takes longer than planned. Strategy: management attention is pulled from the home market. Regulation and macro: different employment rules, exchange rates. Naming two or three specific risks, and how to reduce each one, sounds far more thoughtful than "there are some risks".

How it sounds in an interview

The main risks are that demand is lower than we think and that rivals react. To reduce them, I'd start with a pilot in one city and agree clear targets before expanding.

Use it lightly

Treat this as a prompt for your own thinking, not a script. Pick the parts that matter for this client, say why, and leave the rest out. A short, relevant list beats a complete one every time.
outro: Small things like this add up. Try it in your next practice case and notice how it changes the conversation. All of these sit on the free frameworks page, next to the 11 core trees.
